name: Bilal Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle carer's allowance claims at the Dunmore benefits office, for people looking after a sick parent or a disabled child. I check their hours, their earnings, the person they care for, and I sort out the payment. I use AI every day: I've set up my own templates that pull the numbers into the letter, and I finish my list by three most days. What I enjoy is ringing a carer to say it's approved. What wears me out is the system logging me out every twenty minutes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Amina last year. She's a nursery assistant, and we're hoping for a baby in the next couple of years. We rent a small flat near my uncle's grocery shop, where I still help out on Sundays. Savings are thin, maybe three weeks, because the wedding took everything. Dunmore's a small place: this office, the hospital and shops, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and people who ignore it are missing out. I'd show colleagues my templates. I'd say in the community that hard work still matters more than gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the job's safe, which is good for the baby plans. But we're still on a low wage with three weeks in the bank, and that bothers me more than AI ever did. I'd want to start building something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and teach others my templates. I'd help my uncle put his shop orders and stock on a simple AI system, and maybe charge other shops on the high street for the same. Amina and I would aim for two months' savings before trying for a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about work, restless about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge other shops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe fifty a month to set up their ordering and keep it running. Three or four shops would make a real difference to us. My uncle says the barber and the bakery would sign up if he told them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the baby plans wait for the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd agree a number, two months of rent and bills, and then go for it. Amina thinks I'm too careful. My father had nothing when I was born, and he always said don't start a family on credit.

say: I'd call AI a **useful tool** that people ignore at their cost.
I'd say **hard work** still matters more than gadgets.
think: The job's safe, which is good for our **baby plans**.
A **low wage** with three weeks saved bothers me more than AI.
do: **Set up** AI ordering for his uncle's shop and sell it to others.
**Save** two months of bills before trying for a baby.
S0.quote: My father had nothing when I was born, and he always said don't start a family on credit.
fieldNote: He's already **building** a side business from his AI habit.
His **family plans** are tied to a savings target.
Traditional values show in his father's **no credit** rule.

steps.text: Set up AI stock ordering in his uncle's grocery shop
Charge high street shops fifty a month for ordering setup
Save two months of bills before trying for a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to learn. The government should stop paying people to stand still and help them retrain into real work. I'd say it to friends and I'd post it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the carer's allowance team shrinks a lot, because the checking is easy for software. I'd probably be one of the people running the new system, so I'm not too worried for myself. My real chance is the side business, because every small shop will want this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the new tools at the office, to keep my job while it lasts. I'd sign up the barber, the bakery and the chemist in the first six months. If it grew, I'd go part-time at the office and put the money into a proper laptop and software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little worried about the people who'll be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be left behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okonkwo on my team, who's been there thirty years and won't touch the templates. She's kind and she's slow. I'd try to help her, but I can't make her want to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the government should stop paying people to stand still. Isn't that what you're paid to administer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I see both sides every day. Carers aren't standing still, they're working harder than me. But I'd want help to go into training and work, not just a payment that never changes.

say: I'd call this a **chance** for anyone willing to learn.
I'd say government should fund **retraining**, not people standing still.
think: The **carer's allowance** team will shrink because the checking is easy.
My real chance is the **side business** with local shops.

feel: Mostly **excited**, a little **worried** for colleagues left behind.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the new AI tools at the Dunmore office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast, and the people who run the country need to get a grip. Families and small businesses need breathing room. I'd say that loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and my office job is gone, and so is my side business, because the shops won't need me to set up AI that sets itself up. Everything I was good at, the AI is better at. And we'd just be planning a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into my uncle's shop full-time, because people still come in for bread and a chat, and the shelf-stacking robots are three years away. I'd try to buy into the shop with my uncle, using whatever redundancy money I got. We'd put the baby off a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I always thought being quick to learn would keep me safe from AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amina about putting off the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gently, at home, and she'd cry. Then she'd say we'd have managed, and maybe she's right. But I won't start a family with no job and three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after the robots arrive, around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the shop has to be something a robot can't be: the place where you hear the news and buy halal meat from someone you know. I'd bet on the community side. I don't have a better plan than that.

say: I'd say leaders need to **get a grip** on the pace.
I'd say families and **small businesses** need breathing room.
think: Both my office job and **side business** vanish in two years.
Everything I was good at, the **AI is better** at.
do: **Buy into** the shop with any redundancy money.
**Put off** trying for a baby for a year or two.
feel: **Shaken** that being quick to learn didn't keep him safe.
S2.quote: I always thought being quick to learn would keep me safe from AI.
fieldNote: Fast AGI **wipes out** both his job and his business idea.
He bets on **community** in the shop to outlast the robots.
He'd **delay a baby**, keeping his father's rule.

steps.text: Work full-time in his uncle's grocery shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people take responsibility for themselves. Don't wait for the government to save you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me maybe three good years of the side business, then I'd need the shop. That's enough to save something and buy in properly. It's not safe, but it's something I can build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the AI ordering business hard for two or three years, maybe ten shops. I'd save the profits toward buying half the shop from my uncle by 2030. Then I'd put in self-checkouts and AI stock ordering so it runs lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the baby plans change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still go ahead, maybe a year later than we'd hoped. With the business running, I'd feel all right about it. Amina would want to stop work for a bit, and I'd want to be able to say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you rely on, if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. My uncle, my brothers, Amina's parents. We're a family that pulls together, and that matters more than any benefit payment.

I'd tell people **not to wait** for the government.
think: I'd get about **three good years** from the side business.
After that I'd need the **shop**, which I can build.

fieldNote: He builds a **ladder**: side business first, then the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone with ambition. Learn, save, build something. Don't sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is good for me. I'd have a proper business by 2030 and part of the shop, with a baby or two by then. The robots come for the shelves in 2039, but by then I'd own the place rather than work in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the office a few more years and lead the AI rollout there. I'd grow the shop setup business steadily and buy into the shop. Amina and I would try for a baby once we hit two months' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. A little uneasy, but excited too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big supermarkets could squeeze the small shops out before any of this. That's my real worry, more than AI. A corner shop lives on loyalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your child about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something useful, work hard, and own something. A job can be taken away, but a family business you build yourself is harder to take.

I'd tell people to **learn, save and build** instead of waiting.

A **proper business** by 2030 and a baby or two seem within reach.
do: **Lead** the AI rollout at the office for a few more years.
**Grow** the shop setup business and buy into the **shop**.
**Try for a baby** once savings reach two months.
feel: Pretty **calm**, a little uneasy, and **excited** too.
S4.quote: A job can be taken away, but a family business you build yourself is harder to take.

His real fear shifts to **big supermarkets**, not AI.
He'd pass on a **work and own** message to his child.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my job and my business idea at the same time, right when we're planning a family. What would help is cheap loans for small family businesses and less red tape for anyone trying to start one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what people want to own, not just where they want to work. Lots of people my age would rather build a small shop or a trade than wait for a pay rise. Nobody asks us that.

headlineQuote: Lots of people my age would rather build a small shop or a trade than wait for a pay rise.
portrait: Bilal is 27, handling **carer's allowance** claims in a small town, newly married and hoping for a baby.
He uses AI **every day** and is turning it into a side business for local shops.
He believes in **self-reliance** and family, yet sees how hard carers work.
Fast AGI **shakes him** by erasing both his job and his business idea.
With more time he plans to **own** his uncle's grocery shop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, taking his job and side business as they plan a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** and less red tape for small family businesses.
